header.tag_why: The CFO compared rates only, and no Fernbrook-specific cost of failed orders reached him, so our value case never competed with the rate.

messaging_changes.current_line: Customers see an average uplift in authorization rates with Authorization Boost and Adaptive Acceptance.
messaging_changes.change: For ecommerce leaders with high-value orders: Orders dying at the last step cost you sales on your biggest baskets. Authorization Boost and Adaptive Acceptance recover those orders, and we'll show you what each recovered order is worth to your business.
messaging_changes.why: Martin's 'same thing' objection came after the average-uplift slide failed to describe the loss in his terms, so the customer's own language about lost big-basket orders should replace the generic average.

messaging_changes.current_line: Recover failed payments automatically with smart retries.
messaging_changes.change: For ecommerce teams losing sales at checkout: Recover the orders where the card says no, starting with your big baskets. Smart retries run automatically on each failed payment.
messaging_changes.why: The customer described the problem as orders dying at the last step on high-value baskets, so the recovery line should name that loss directly rather than describe the feature alone.

messaging_changes.change: For champions presenting to a CFO: A decline-cost business case built from your own payment export, showing lost order value next to gateway fees and chargebacks, which we can produce within days of receiving the export.
messaging_changes.why: Farah offered the decline analysis that would have answered the CFO's objection, Lucy asked for something to hand Martin, and the record shows nothing from us on failure cost reached him, so a fast standard leave-behind fills that gap.

messaging_changes.change: For buyers comparing processors: Compare total cost, including the value of declined orders, before discussing our rate. A rate counter alone does not change the value of the orders you are losing.
messaging_changes.why: The incumbent's only move was a rate cut that then replaced every other topic in the emails, so a total-cost framing gives the prospect a second number to weigh against any rate offer.

trigger.insight: The deal started from a failure rate the customer pulled from its own dashboard, concentrated on large orders. That is the strongest number in this deal, and the rep treated it as background rather than as the business case. Nothing in the record shows we turned it into a dollar figure.
trigger.messaging: Lead with the prospect's own failure rate and the value of the orders it hits, not generic uplift averages.

message.messaging: Ground the acceptance-uplift claim (M4) in a Fernbrook-specific number that the prospect can take to its CFO.

decided.insight: The loss arrived after Lucy's meeting with the CFO, which means the rep's forecast of a formality was wrong. The objection the customer quotes is a value objection ('the same thing'), not a pure price one, and the rate-only one-pager gave it a place to land. The rep's closing claim that the rate is what killed it contradicts his own 'maybe not only the rate'.
decided.messaging: Make the side-by-side comparison show total cost, including gateway fees and decline losses, before any rate line appears.

gaps.insight: Farah offered the analysis that would have answered Martin's objection, and the rep declined it to save time. When the customer then asked for a CFO leave-behind, we sent generic materials, and the rep's own account says nothing from us on failure cost reached Martin. The gap was a missing business case, and the rep chose speed over building it.
gaps.messaging: Offer a fast, standard decline-cost business case built from a short export, so the SE can produce it within days rather than a quarter.

language.insight: The customer describes lost sales at the payment step, a revenue problem tied to specific high-value orders. Our pitch speaks in terms of knocked-back orders and average uplift, which is our frame. Martin's 'same thing' shows the CFO was comparing two rates because nothing on our side described the loss in his terms.
language.messaging: Rewrite M4 and M10 in the customer's words: orders dying at the last step, and what each lost big-basket sale is worth.

gaps.question: Did Martin ever see any figure on what failed orders were costing Fernbrook?
gaps.follow_up: Ask Lucy directly whether anything about lost-order value was shown to Martin or the controller.

gaps.question: What exactly was on the controller's one-pager, and did it include the gateway fee or chargeback costs?
gaps.follow_up: Ask Lucy for a copy of the one-pager or a description of its line items.

gaps.question: If we had matched the rate, would finance have approved, and what was the real gate?
gaps.follow_up: Ask Lucy and the IT lead whether finance approval alone would have been enough, or whether spring timing was the binding constraint.

gaps.question: What, if anything, did Martin say after the meeting, and did he respond to the one-pager directly?
gaps.follow_up: Ask Lucy what Martin said in her meeting, in his own words if she has them.

gaps.question: Did Farah's proposed decline export ever get approved or requested internally?
gaps.follow_up: Ask Farah whether Lucy ever asked IT for the three-month export after the meeting.

close.rep_takeaway: A dashboard-verified failure rate was the strongest asset in this deal, and it never became a Fernbrook number. Before the CFO sees a price, build the decline-cost case from the customer's own data, even when the timeline is short, and don't turn down the SE's value analysis to protect the schedule.
